title: Inter-Domain Routing & BGP Basics
summary: See how autonomous systems exchange routes across the internet, BGP's path-vector model, and why BGP incidents — route hijacks, major outages — keep happening.

slides.sectionTitle: The internet is a network of networks
slides.markdown: Everything covered so far in Routing happens *within* one organization's network. The internet itself is thousands of independently-run networks stitched together by **BGP** — a protocol built on business trust and policy as much as on pure math, which is exactly why BGP incidents make headline news.

An **Autonomous System (AS)** is a network (or group of networks) under one administrative control with a unified routing policy — an ISP, a large cloud provider, a university. Each AS is identified by a globally unique **ASN** (Autonomous System Number), assigned by a regional registry.

The internet, structurally, is just tens of thousands of ASes agreeing to exchange routes with each other — there's no central authority deciding global paths, only bilateral agreements between neighboring ASes.

| | IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol) | EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Within one AS | Between different ASes |
| Examples | OSPF, RIP | BGP (the only one in practical use) |
| Trust model | All routers under one admin | Independent organizations, need policy control |
| Optimizes for | Shortest/fastest path | Business relationships as much as path length |

**How to decide which applies:** if the question is about routing inside one company's network, think OSPF/IGP; if it's about how traffic crosses between different organizations' networks on the public internet, think BGP/EGP.

BGP is neither distance-vector nor link-state — it's a **path-vector** protocol: instead of a plain hop count or cost, each route carries its **full AS-path** — the ordered list of every AS it has passed through.

This serves two purposes at once: it's the primary input to path selection (shorter AS-paths are generally preferred, though not the only factor), and it's a built-in loop-prevention mechanism — if an AS sees its own number already in a route's path, it discards that route immediately, since accepting it would create a loop.

BGP runs in two modes depending on whether peers share an AS:

![eBGP peering between two autonomous systems, with iBGP distributing the learned routes internally within each AS](assets/ebgp-ibgp.svg)

**eBGP** (external) connects routers in *different* ASes — where actual inter-organization exchange happens. **iBGP** (internal) then spreads what was learned to every router inside the same AS, so they forward consistently.

assets.alt: eBGP peering between two autonomous systems, with iBGP distributing the learned routes internally within each AS

slides.sectionTitle: How BGP picks a best path
slides.markdown:
When multiple routes exist to the same destination, BGP works through a sequence of tie-breakers (simplified): highest **local preference** (a policy value set by your own AS), then shortest **AS-path length**, then lowest-origin-type, then several further tie-breakers down to lowest router ID.

The critical thing to internalize: **path length is only the second criterion**, not the first — an administrator's local preference (a business/policy decision) overrides pure path length every time. BGP optimizes for policy first, distance second.

As a route propagates outward from its origin, every AS along the way **prepends its own number** before passing it on:

![A route advertisement growing its AS-path as it propagates from AS 100 outward through AS 200 and AS 300](assets/route-propagation.svg)

By the time a route reaches a distant AS, its AS-path is a full record of every network it passed through — the basis for path selection and loop detection.

assets.alt: A route advertisement growing its AS-path as it propagates from AS 100 outward through AS 200 and AS 300

slides.sectionTitle: BGP is policy, not just math
slides.markdown:
ISPs don't route purely on shortest AS-path — they filter and prefer routes based on **business relationships**: a paying customer's routes get preferred over a settlement-free peer's; a route through a competitor might be deliberately deprioritized or filtered even if shorter.

This is why two seemingly equivalent paths across the internet can perform very differently — the "best" BGP path reflects contractual and commercial decisions at least as much as it reflects network topology.

BGP has essentially **no built-in verification** that an AS advertising a route actually owns that address space — an AS accidentally or maliciously advertising routes it doesn't own can **hijack** traffic destined there, sometimes globally, within minutes.

Several well-known internet-wide outages trace back to exactly this — a misconfigured router announcing routes it shouldn't, and much of the internet believing it. **RPKI** (cryptographically verifying who may originate a prefix) exists to reduce this risk — see [Common Network Attacks](common-network-attacks).

| | BGP | OSPF |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Between organizations (internet-wide) | Within one organization |
| Trust model | Independent parties, verify little by default | All routers under one trusted admin |
| Path metric philosophy | Policy and business relationships first, path length second | Pure cost/bandwidth-based shortest path |
| Failure blast radius | Can affect large parts of the global internet | Contained within one organization's network |

**How to decide which is relevant:** if the scenario involves crossing organizational boundaries on the public internet, think BGP; if it's entirely inside one company's infrastructure, think OSPF.

**Anycast** — the same IP announced from multiple physical locations, traffic reaching whichever is "closest" — is built directly on BGP. Multiple data centers advertise the identical prefix; BGP's normal best-path selection naturally routes each user to whichever location their ISP's path prefers.

This is how large CDNs and DNS resolvers (`8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`) serve one address globally from dozens of locations — see [Load Balancing & CDNs](cdn-edge-caching).

slides.subTitle: "The return path should be the same as the outbound path"
slides.markdown:
A common mistake is assuming your traffic to a server and its response back to you follow the same path in reverse. They don't have to — each direction is an independent BGP path decision, potentially made by different ASes with different policies, so the forward and return paths can genuinely differ in hop count, latency, and even which providers they cross.

This matters practically when diagnosing latency: a `traceroute` from you to a server only shows *one* direction — the return path could be entirely different, and tools that assume symmetry can mislead you about where a real bottleneck sits.
